name: Differential Privacy
description: Differentially private mechanisms, analytics, and deployments, including local DP.

uss.narrative:
The earliest USENIX Security work in this list grappled with two practical realities of differential privacy (DP): how well it actually protects machine learning, and how local DP behaves once it leaves the textbook. "Evaluating Differentially Private Machine Learning in Practice" (USENIX 2019) sounded an early, widely-cited warning that the privacy budget epsilon is often set so loosely that real guarantees evaporate, while "When the Signal is in the Noise: Exploiting Diffix's Sticky Noise" (USENIX 2019) attacked a deployed anonymization system to show how fragile non-rigorous schemes are. In parallel, the local DP (LDP) thread began maturing toward utility: "Utility-Optimized Local Differential Privacy Mechanisms for Distribution Estimation" (USENIX 2019) and "PCKV" (USENIX 2020) pushed LDP beyond simple homogeneous frequency estimation toward correlated key-value and sensitivity-aware data.

The early 2020s broadened DP from a theoretical tool into a systems and deployment problem. Several papers married DP with cryptography and distributed settings: "Secure Multi-party Computation of Differentially Private Median" (USENIX 2020), "How to Make Private Distributed Cardinality Estimation Practical, and Get Differential Privacy for Free" (USENIX 2021), and "Batched Differentially Private Information Retrieval" (USENIX 2022) all showed DP composing with secure computation. Application breadth also exploded, from software telemetry in "Differentially-Private Control-Flow Node Coverage for Software Usage Analysis" (USENIX 2020), to eye-tracking in "Kalεido" (USENIX 2021), to synthetic data and graphs in "PrivSyn" (USENIX 2021) and "Locally Differentially Private Analysis of Graph Statistics" (USENIX 2021). Crucially, this period also exposed LDP's attack surface: "Data Poisoning Attacks to Local Differential Privacy Protocols" (USENIX 2021) showed that the same untrusted-aggregator model that protects users lets malicious users skew results.

By the mid-2020s the field turned reflective and human-facing. "What Are the Chances? Explaining the Epsilon Parameter in Differential Privacy" (USENIX 2023) tackled the usability gap the 2019 evaluation paper foreshadowed, asking how to communicate epsilon to real people, while DP moved deep into modern ML with "PrivateFL" (USENIX 2023) for federated learning, "PrivGraph" (USENIX 2023) for graph publication, and generative methods like "dp-promise: Differentially Private Diffusion Probabilistic Models for Image Synthesis" (USENIX 2024).

The current frontier, dominated by USENIX 2024-2025, splits in two directions. One is rigorous privacy auditing and tighter accounting: "Efficient Privacy Auditing in Federated Learning" (USENIX 2024), "Closed-Form Bounds for DP-SGD against Record-level Inference" (USENIX 2024), "Privacy Audit as Bits Transmission: (Im)possibilities for Audit by One Run" (USENIX 2025), and "General-Purpose f-DP Estimation and Auditing in a Black-Box Setting" (USENIX 2025) push toward empirically and formally verifying claimed guarantees. The other is scaling DP to large modern models and refining LDP utility, seen in "Unlocking the Power of Differentially Private Zeroth-order Optimization for Fine-tuning LLMs" (USENIX 2025), "Addressing Sensitivity Distinction in Local Differential Privacy" (USENIX 2025), and the reality check "SoK: Can Synthetic Images Replace Real Data?" (USENIX 2025). The arc runs from questioning whether DP delivers in practice, through broad deployment, to a mature insistence on auditing what was deployed.

ndss.narrative:
The earliest work in this collection shows differential privacy arriving as a tool for concrete, high-stakes data rather than an abstract guarantee. "MBeacon: Privacy-Preserving Beacons for DNA Methylation Data" (NDSS 2019) applied DP to genomic beacon services to blunt membership inference, while "Private Continual Release of Real-Valued Data Streams" (NDSS 2019) tackled the streaming setting, where noise must be added continually without the privacy budget collapsing over time. Both signal a field moving from single static queries toward realistic, ongoing data release.

Around 2020 the center of gravity shifted toward local differential privacy (LDP) and adversarial settings. "Locally Differentially Private Frequency Estimation with Consistency" (NDSS 2020) made LDP analytics genuinely deployable by producing consistent estimates, and "Secure Sublinear Time Differentially Private Median Computation" (NDSS 2020) pushed for efficiency in distributed private analysis, while "Adversarial Classification Under Differential Privacy" (NDSS 2020) began asking how DP holds up against active attackers. By 2022 the field was wiring DP into larger systems: "Local and Central Differential Privacy for Robustness and Privacy in Federated Learning" (NDSS 2022) weighed local versus central noise inside federated training, and papers like "Privacy in Urban Sensing with Instrumented Fleets" and "On Utility and Privacy in Synthetic Genomic Data" (both NDSS 2022) probed the always-present tension between usable data and real protection.

By 2025 the community turned a critical eye on its own foundations. "Revisiting EM-based Estimation for Locally Differentially Private Protocols" (NDSS 2025) reexamined the core estimation problem underlying years of LDP work, "Delay-allowed Differentially Private Data Stream Release" (NDSS 2025) revisited streaming with a fresh utility angle, and "On the Robustness of LDP Protocols for Numerical Attributes under Data Poisoning Attacks" (NDSS 2025) showed that LDP protocols can themselves be manipulated by poisoning — reframing the goal from privacy alone to privacy plus robustness.

The most recent NDSS 2026 papers spread DP across nearly every modern data modality and pressure-test its guarantees. "To Shuffle or not to Shuffle: Auditing DP-SGD with Shuffling" audits the gap between claimed and actual privacy in the dominant private-training pipeline, while "Augmented Shuffle Differential Privacy Protocols for Large-Domain Categorical and Key-Value Data" and "When Focus Enhances Utility: Target Range LDP Frequency Estimation and Unknown Item Discovery" refine the shuffle and local models for richer data. A wave of generative and estimation work — "PrivORL: Differentially Private Synthetic Dataset for Offline Reinforcement Learning," "PrivCode: When Code Generation Meets Differential Privacy," "PrivATE: Differentially Private Average Treatment Effect Estimation for Observational Data," and "Revisiting Differentially Private Hyper-parameter Tuning" — pushes DP into synthetic data, code, and causal inference, and "Convergent Privacy Framework for Multi-layer GNNs through Contractive Message Passing" (NDSS 2026) brings rigorous accounting to graph neural networks. The area now stands as a mature toolkit being carefully audited, hardened against adversaries, and stretched to cover streams, graphs, generative models, and complex learning pipelines.

sp.narrative:
The earliest work in this list treats differential privacy (DP) mainly as a data-collection problem, especially in the local model where users perturb their own data before it ever leaves their device. "Locally Differentially Private Frequent Itemset Mining" (S&P 2018) shows how to mine patterns from user responses without a trusted aggregator, and "PrivKV: Key-Value Data Collection with Local Differential Privacy" (S&P 2019) extends LDP to richer key-value records. In parallel, a machine-learning thread opens up: "Differentially Private Model Publishing for Deep Learning" and "Towards Practical Differentially Private Convex Optimization" (both S&P 2019) push DP into model training, while "Certified Robustness to Adversarial Examples with Differential Privacy" (S&P 2019) repurposes the DP toolkit for a completely different goal, provable robustness, signaling how versatile the framework had become.

Around 2020-2021 the field turns a critical eye on its own guarantees. Foundational and usability questions surface with "SoK: Differential Privacy as a Causal Property" and "Towards Effective Differential Privacy Communication for Users' Data Sharing Decision and Comprehension" (both S&P 2020), while a wave of adversarial and auditing work asks whether DP actually delivers what it promises. "Adversary Instantiation: Lower Bounds for Differentially Private Machine Learning" (S&P 2021) measures real privacy leakage against theoretical bounds, "Manipulation Attacks in Local Differential Privacy" (S&P 2021) shows malicious users can skew LDP aggregates, and "DP-Sniper" (S&P 2021) automatically discovers DP violations with classifiers. This scrutiny sharpens further in "Are We There Yet? Timing and Floating-Point Attacks on Differential Privacy Systems" (S&P 2022), which breaks deployed mechanisms through implementation side channels rather than flawed math.

The mid-2020s broaden DP to new data types and deployment realities while professionalizing the tooling for checking it. Graph and streaming settings mature with "Preserving Node-level Privacy in Graph Neural Networks," "Time-Aware Projections: Truly Node-Private Graph Statistics under Continual Observation," and "DPI: Ensuring Strict Differential Privacy for Infinite Data Streaming" (all S&P 2024), while "SoK: Privacy-Preserving Data Synthesis" (S&P 2024) organizes the fast-growing synthetic-data literature. Auditing becomes a first-class engineering discipline through "Eureka: A General Framework for Black-box Differential Privacy Estimators" and "DP-Auditorium: A Large-Scale Library for Auditing Differential Privacy" (both S&P 2024). Real deployments also reach the venue: "Differentially Private Release of Israel's National Registry of Live Births" (S&P 2025) documents a concrete government release, echoing the earlier census debate in "Differential Privacy and Swapping" (S&P 2022).

The most recent work (S&P 2026) reads as a field auditing its own promises in production and rethinking its foundations. "Auditing Apple's DifferentialPrivacy.framework: Implementation Bugs, Misconfigurations, and Practical Risks" scrutinizes one of the largest real-world LDP deployments and finds concrete gaps, while "Making Privacy Public: Toward a Differential Privacy Deployment Registry" argues for shared accountability across all such deployments. Alongside this, foundational refinements continue with "Decomposition-Based Optimal Bounds for Privacy Amplification via Shuffling" and "Privacy-Conscious Algorithm Design Via PAC Privacy," and the framework keeps colliding with new threat models in "Beyond Indistinguishability: Measuring Extraction Risk in LLM APIs" and "Hadal: Centralized Label DP without a Trusted Party." Taken together, the trajectory runs from inventing private collection and training mechanisms, through years of adversarial stress-testing, to today's emphasis on auditing, transparency, and honest accounting of what DP delivers once it is actually deployed.

ccs.narrative:
Differential privacy research at CCS has grown from foundational mechanism design to applied DP in ML and graph analytics. The 2018 cohort tackled a broad range of settings: Detecting Violations of Differential Privacy (CCS 2018) automated correctness testing for DP implementations, Utility-Aware Synthesis of Differentially Private and Attack-Resilient Location Traces (CCS 2018) addressed location privacy with utility constraints, and CALM: Consistent Adaptive Local Marginal for Marginal Release under Local Differential Privacy (CCS 2018) improved local DP for marginal query release.

Graph DP became a distinct sub-area starting in 2019: Analyzing Subgraph Statistics from Extended Local Views with Decentralized Differential Privacy (CCS 2019) applied decentralized DP to social graph analysis, and Locally Private Graph Neural Networks (CCS 2021) extended local DP to GNN training to protect node features. Private Summation in the Multi-Message Shuffle Model (CCS 2020) explored the shuffle model as an intermediate privacy tier between local and central DP.

From 2022, DP intersected with the LLM boom. DP-Forward: Fine-tuning and Inference on Language Models with Differential Privacy in Forward Pass (CCS 2023) introduced forward-pass perturbation to protect against embedding-level inference attacks during fine-tuning. Evaluations of Machine Learning Privacy Defenses are Misleading (CCS 2024) questioned the reliability of DP evaluation benchmarks, pointing toward methodological reform.

top4.narrative:
The earliest work in this list, clustered in 2018, split along two lines that would define the field. One line pushed local differential privacy (LDP) toward richer data types, moving beyond simple counts to "Locally Differentially Private Frequent Itemset Mining" (S&P 2018) and marginal release with "CALM: Consistent Adaptive Local Marginal for Marginal Release under Local Differential Privacy" (CCS 2018), plus privacy for structured data like "Utility-Aware Synthesis of Differentially Private and Attack-Resilient Location Traces" (CCS 2018). The other line turned a skeptical eye on the mechanisms themselves: "Detecting Violations of Differential Privacy" and "DP-Finder: Finding Differential Privacy Violations by Sampling and Optimization" (both CCS 2018) built tooling to catch buggy or dishonest DP implementations, while "Tight on Budget?: Tight Bounds for r-Fold Approximate Differential Privacy" (CCS 2018) sharpened the accounting math.

The pivot toward machine learning arrived forcefully in 2019. "Certified Robustness to Adversarial Examples with Differential Privacy" (S&P 2019) reframed DP as a tool for model robustness, while "Evaluating Differentially Private Machine Learning in Practice" (USENIX 2019) and "Differentially Private Model Publishing for Deep Learning" (S&P 2019) stress-tested whether DP-SGD's guarantees held up in real training pipelines. LDP kept advancing in parallel with "PrivKV: Key-Value Data Collection with Local Differential Privacy" (S&P 2019). By the early 2020s the community was maturing on two fronts at once: the shuffle model emerged as a middle ground between central and local trust, developed in "Private Summation in the Multi-Message Shuffle Model" (CCS 2020) and "On the Rényi Differential Privacy of the Shuffle Model" (CCS 2021); and adversarial thinking deepened with "Adversary Instantiation: Lower Bounds for Differentially Private Machine Learning" (S&P 2021) and "Manipulation Attacks in Local Differential Privacy" (S&P 2021), which showed malicious users could poison LDP aggregates.

A striking shift in this window was the arrival of the human element and of implementation-level attacks. Usability studies like "'I need a better description': An Investigation Into User Expectations For Differential Privacy" (CCS 2021) and "What Are the Chances? Explaining the Epsilon Parameter in Differential Privacy" (USENIX 2023) asked whether anyone could actually understand epsilon, while "Are We There Yet? Timing and Floating-Point Attacks on Differential Privacy Systems" (S&P 2022) showed that side channels can leak what the math promises to hide. Meanwhile DP folded into modern ML deployment through "DP-Forward: Fine-tuning and Inference on Language Models with Differential Privacy in Forward Pass" (CCS 2023) and "PrivateFL: Accurate, Differentially Private Federated Learning via Personalized Data Transformation" (USENIX 2023), and the field began taking stock with "SoK: Privacy-Preserving Data Synthesis" (S&P 2024).

The most recent work, dominated by NDSS 2026 and S&P 2026, shows the area both consolidating and specializing. Auditing has become first-class, with "To Shuffle or not to Shuffle: Auditing DP-SGD with Shuffling" (NDSS 2026) revisiting whether common training shortcuts undermine claimed guarantees, echoed by "Revisiting Differentially Private Hyper-parameter Tuning" (NDSS 2026). Generative and code-oriented DP has exploded — "PrivORL: Differentially Private Synthetic Dataset for Offline Reinforcement Learning" and "PrivCode: When Code Generation Meets Differential Privacy" (both NDSS 2026) — while the shuffle and LDP lines continue in "Augmented Shuffle Differential Privacy Protocols for Large-Domain Categorical and Key-Value Data" and "When Focus Enhances Utility: Target Range LDP Frequency Estimation and Unknown Item Discovery" (both NDSS 2026). The frontier now reaches into causal inference with "PrivATE: Differentially Private Average Treatment Effect Estimation for Observational Data" (NDSS 2026), graph learning with "Convergent Privacy Framework for Multi-layer GNNs through Contractive Message Passing" (NDSS 2026), and relaxed trust models with "Hadal: Centralized Label DP without a Trusted Party" (S&P 2026), signaling a field that has moved from proving basic mechanisms to hardening, auditing, and embedding DP across the full ML and analytics stack.
